results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 68 outline summaries match the controlling idea of the aligned spec paragraph, in spec order (p01-p68).
The outliner marked no unit as two_ideas.

Every unit traces to S1-S6: scene and wms to S1/S5, the fulfillment-order units to S2, stock to S3, confirmation and wholesale to S4, the working day and in-practice to S5, choices and stages to S6, failures to S2-S5.
All other evidence (tables, Figures 1-8, the GS1 and Zalando quotations, the vendor sources and the Kestrel & Pine cases) is introduced and its point stated.

results.draft_locus: What a Warehouse Management System Does ¶2
results.quote: Picqer describes batch pick lists and planned routes, while Manhattan's Order Streaming coordinates wholesale, retail and direct orders
results.finding: The Manhattan source is cited in a paragraph about how picking methods organize travel, but what it shows (coordinating wholesale, retail and direct orders) is not about cluster or batch picking and is not connected to the controlling idea; a flow reader (flowB) also reported the vendor list as breaking the explanation.

Every declared transition_in is expressed at its boundary (e.g. 'similarly' p02, 'Then Daniel shows ... but' p08, 'Those steps ... lead to' p13, 'Both models put acceptance before the work, for a physical reason' p19, 'Beyond the Black Friday queue' p55).

Both readers describe problem -> mechanism (WMS, then interfaces in prerequisite order) -> options and stages -> worked cases -> failures, which agrees with the declared prerequisite_order with problem_solution (scene/in-practice) and comparison (choices/stages). No section's position was 'unclear'. Points both readers raised about Waypoint, Duiven, on-hand and EDI concern terms on intent.audience.already_knows (Waypoint decisions W1-W8, Kestrel & Pine, on hand from Part II, the EDI gloss) and are not material for the declared audience; the deferred Black Friday cause was judged deliberate by both.

results.quote: The same contract applies one level down, inside an automated warehouse.
results.finding: Both readers found the automation section the weakest placement: Duiven has no automation, the section is hypothetical, and it interrupts the move from what the warehouse must exchange to who runs it; both proposed moving it after Across Scale Stages. flowA also had to work out which 'same contract' was meant, two subsections back. Both call the position signalled and workable, so the cost is mild, but the order itself causes it.
results.corroborated_by: flowB item 2 and 4: Automation 'Partly clear' ... 'Move Warehouse Automation and Robotics after Across Scale Stages ... It is hypothetical for Duiven and interrupts the move from contract to buying choice.'

results.draft_locus: How the Warehouse Connects to Everything Else ¶10
results.quote: The same contract, both ways, can survive Waypoint decision W2: an OMS replaces the shop platform as the sender in Q4 2027 without changing the warehouse's responsibilities.
results.finding: Both readers re-read this sentence: 'can survive' hedges what the spec states as a fact, and 'both ways' has no clear referent. State plainly that the contract (instruction in, confirmations out) stays the same when the OMS becomes the sender.
results.corroborated_by: flowB item 3: "'The same contract, both ways, can survive Waypoint decision W2' is unclear: I could not tell what 'both ways' means."

results.draft_locus: How the Warehouse Connects to Everything Else ¶12
results.quote: The rule I give every merchant
results.finding: The first-person voice arrives unannounced, and the same paragraph's last sentence packs two incidents (the App That Wrote Stock of March 2026 and the May 2027 reconciliation, a date after the April 2027 scene) into one long clause; flowA re-read it, flowB re-read it to check the timeline.
results.corroborated_by: flowB item 3: "'The rule I give every merchant' is the first time the author's voice appears" and "'the first reconciliation of May 2027' comes in a scene set during an April 2027 visit ... I re-read it to check the timeline."

results.draft_locus: The Choices: Who Runs the Warehouse Software ¶8
results.quote: Kestrel & Pine shows where that leads: its shop platform, its ERP and its warehouse report each count orders by a different definition.
results.finding: Neither reader could connect this example to the warning before it (never let the WMS become a second order system); the draft does not say how the three order counts follow from that, so it reads as a new, unfollowed claim at the end of the recommendation.
results.corroborated_by: flowB item 3: "I could not connect this to the warning that comes just before it, about the WMS becoming a second order system."

results.draft_locus: How the Warehouse Connects to Everything Else ¶17
results.quote: A parcel for Eva and a pallet for Bergzicht Outdoor leave the same building through different processes.
results.finding: Bergzicht Outdoor is named with no word on who it is; both readers had to infer from the later chargeback paragraph that it is a retail (wholesale) customer. A short appositive ('Kestrel & Pine's retail customer') fixes it.
results.corroborated_by: flowB item 3: "'a pallet for Bergzicht Outdoor' introduces Bergzicht with no word on who it is. I inferred it is a retail customer only from the chargeback paragraph."

results.finding: The callout names The First Snowfall, Schrödinger's Order and The Phantom Stock, but the body never uses these names and uses its own incident names (the Queue That Waited, the Three-Status Order, App That Wrote Stock), so the reader has to map the two naming systems. Reported by flowB only; minor.

results.draft_locus: What a Warehouse Management System Does ¶4
results.quote: a reminder to count rather than a rate to assume. That makes it Duiven's **system of record**
results.finding: One bullet packs a study, a caveat and a definition; 'it' (the WMS) is ambiguous after the study sentence. Reported by flowB only; minor.

results.draft_locus: How the Warehouse Connects to Everything Else ¶20
results.quote: €250 per order below 90% delivered on time and in full on an order line
results.finding: flowA had to re-read the penalty sentence to parse it. Reported by flowA only; minor.

Every does_not_know term is explained at or before first use (location, put-away, slotting, waves, cluster and batch picking, cartonization, cycle counting, AMR, goods-to-person, robotic picking, sortation, WES, WCS, fleet management, the fulfillment-order lifecycle, cut-off, capacity, release policy, SSCC, DESADV/ASN, EDIFACT, marketplace programs and the see-but-not-count location). Terms the flow readers found unexplained (Waypoint W-decisions, on hand, EDI, Duiven) are on already_knows.
Opens on a puzzling scenario (the picker who finds no jacket), then the claim and the roadmap; no weak pattern.
The conclusion synthesizes the three opening faults into one cause and one contract, then sorts what is established, what depends on context and the author's judgement; no weak pattern.
p63 names the common cause and the contract, and states what a merchant should write down before buying a WMS, a 3PL or robots, with the Black Friday remedy.
p63 opens with 'The picker who found no jacket', the opening hook, set against Eva's promise and the Black Friday queue.

Reader places the fault in the order feed (one-at-a-time creation, several calls, vendor rate limit) and in a promise that ignored the real cut-off and queue, and names all four remedies and 'not a faster warehouse'.

Reader gives the idempotency key and reuse of the existing instruction (no second pick list or jacket), and the cancellation as a request the warehouse may refuse, with the order staying in progress, support telling the customer and the item returning.
Reader names the WMS, at pack time, from what was actually packed, never the order or the ERP view, with the €14,200 ASN Chargeback and W6.

From the introduction alone the reader predicted the sections in order (Duiven Black Friday, what a WMS does, fulfillment order, stock, working day, wholesale, automation, four choices, scale, Eva and Black Friday worked through, failures) and the evidence (Kestrel & Pine's Duiven case and vendor and standards documentation).
The reverse outline lists the same 68 controlling ideas in the same order as the spec's paragraphs.
